claim: Random Projections (RP) models have demonstrated high accuracy, efficiency, and scalability for modeling neural population codes.
source: A novel class of models, based on learning to weigh sparse nonlinear Random Projections (RP) of the population, has demonstrated high accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work establishing the performance characteristics of RP models.

claim: RP models have a clear and biologically plausible implementation as shallow neural networks.
source: Importantly, these RP models have a clear and biologically plausible implementation as shallow neural networks.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of RP models, drawing on prior knowledge about their neural circuit implementation.

claim: Reshaped RP models are more accurate and efficient than standard RP models in recapitulating the code of tens of cortical neurons from behaving monkeys.
source: We show that Reshaped RP models are more accurate and efficient than the standard RP models in recapitulating the code of tens of cortical neurons from behaving monkeys.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing model performance on cortical recordings.

claim: Incorporating synaptic normalization in the learning process results in accurate models that are more efficient.
source: Incorporating more biological features and utilizing synaptic normalization in the learning process, results in accurate models that are more efficient.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results showing improved efficiency with synaptic normalization.

claim: Reshaped RP models with synaptic normalization exhibit homeostasis in firing rates and total synaptic weights of projection neurons.
source: Remarkably, these models exhibit homeostasis in firing rates and total synaptic weights of projection neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data showing regulation of firing rates and synaptic weights during learning.

claim: Sparse homeostatic reshaped RP models outperform fully connected neural network models.
source: We further show that these sparse homeostatic reshaped RP models outperform fully connected neural network models.
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance data between sparse and fully connected models.

claim: Synaptic normalization has a dual functional role in neural circuits: maintaining spiking and synaptic homeostasis while concurrently optimizing network performance and efficiency.
source: These findings suggest a dual functional role of synaptic normalization in neural circuits: maintaining spiking and synaptic homeostasis while concurrently optimizing network performance and efficiency in encoding information and learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed properties of the models with synaptic normalization.

claim: Generalized Linear Models have been used to replicate the stimulus-dependent rates of populations of tens of neurons.
source: Models of the directional coupling between neurons, such as Generalized Linear Models, have been used to replicate the stimulus-dependent rates of populations of tens of neurons (Truccolo et al., 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Calabrese et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work using GLMs for neural population modeling.

claim: Maximum entropy models have accurately captured the joint activity patterns of more than 100 neurons using simple statistical features.
source: Maximum entropy models have accurately captured the joint activity patterns of more than 100 neurons, using simple statistical features of the population, like firing rates, pairwise correlations, synchrony, and other low-order statistics (Schneidman et al., 2006; Shlens et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2008; Tkačik et al., 2014; Ganmor et al., 2011; Marre et al., 2009; Ohiorhenuan et al., 2010; Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013; Meshulam et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on maximum entropy models.

claim: Maximum entropy models have been used to characterize the semantic organization of population codes.
source: These models have further been used to characterize the semantic organization of population codes (Ganmor et al., 2015; Tkačik et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Auto-encoder models have been employed to replicate the detailed structure of population activity.
source: Auto-encoder models have been employed to replicate the detailed structure of population activity – yielding generative models that can be used to study the code, but their design is difficult to interpret (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Barrett et al., 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on auto-encoder models.

claim: Scaling statistical models of neural population activity to hundreds of neurons is computationally demanding.
source: Importantly, scaling of these models to hundreds of neurons is computationally demanding (Tkačik et al., 2015; Meshulam et al., 2019; Ganmor et al., 2011), which has been a major challenge in modeling large neural systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work discussing computational challenges.

claim: It is not clear whether the brain relies on or implements statistical models when representing or processing information.
source: While statistical models are invaluable for describing and studying neural codes, it is not clear whether the brain relies on such models or implements them when representing or processing information (Schneidman, 2016; Karpas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations discussing the uncertainty about biological implementation.

claim: If neural circuits implement statistical models that compute the likelihood of their inputs, this would present a realizable mechanism for Bayesian computation and decision making.
source: Yet, if neural circuits do implement such statistical models, and in particular, ones that compute the likelihood of their inputs – this would present a realizable mechanism for real neural circuits to carry Bayesian computation and decision making (Maoz et al., 2020; Vertes and Sahani, 2018; Zemel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a conditional inference supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Both structured architectural features and random connectivity patterns have been suggested to shape computation in neural circuits.
source: Both structured architectural features of neural circuits and random connectivity patterns have been suggested to shape the computation carried out by neural circuits (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Maoz et al., 2020; Haber and Schneidman, 2022a; Kim et al., 2019; Pechuk et al., 2022; Haber and Schneidman, 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on neural circuit architecture.

claim: Competition mechanisms between synapses have been suggested to be important components of computation and learning in artificial neural networks and cortical circuits.
source: Competition mechanisms between synapses or other regularization mechanisms have also been suggested to be important components of computation and learning in artificial neural networks as well as in cortical circuits (Heeger, 1992; Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on synaptic competition.

claim: Homeostatic scaling of synaptic plasticity has been observed in vitro and in vivo at the level of incoming and outgoing synapses.
source: One such mechanism is the homeostatic scaling of synaptic plasticity, which has been observed in vitro and in vivo at the level of incoming synapses to a neuron and outgoing ones (Turrigiano et al., 1998; Keck et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2013; Turrigiano, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: Homeostatic scaling of synaptic plasticity has been commonly attributed to the regulation of firing rates.
source: This mechanism has been commonly attributed to the regulation of firing rates, while its functional implications remain mostly unclear, but of interest computationally and mechanistically (El-Boustani et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2020; Keck et al., 2017; Zenke and Gerstner, 2017; Toyoizumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: Divisive normalization has been suggested as an important component of computations performed by cortical circuits.
source: A related computational feature has been presented by network models that include divisive normalization, suggested as an important component of computations performed by cortical circuits (Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on divisive normalization.

claim: RP models were shown to be highly accurate in recapitulating the detailed spiking patterns of more than 100 neurons in different neural systems.
source: Specifically, we expand the Random Projections (RP) model (Maoz et al., 2020), which was shown to be highly accurate in recapitulating the detailed spiking patterns of more than 100 neurons in different neural systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating RP model accuracy.

claim: RP models require little amounts of training data.
source: Importantly, in addition to being accurate and requiring little amounts of training data, these RP models can be readily implemented by a simple neural circuit model
evidence: This is stated as an established property of RP models based on prior work.

claim: RP models can be readily implemented by a simple neural circuit model.
source: Importantly, in addition to being accurate and requiring little amounts of training data, these RP models can be readily implemented by a simple neural circuit model – suggesting how real neural circuits can learn a statistical model of their own inputs and compute the likelihood of the inputs.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of RP models based on prior work.

claim: Reshaping randomly chosen sparse non-linear projections results in highly accurate models using significantly fewer projections.
source: We show that we can make these models better by 'reshaping' the randomly chosen sparse non-linear projections that they rely on, achieving highly accurate models using significantly fewer projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reshaping of projections that incorporates normalization of synaptic weights during learning results in more accurate and efficient models.
source: We further show that reshaping of projections that incorporates normalization of synaptic weights during learning, results in more accurate models that are also more efficient, and makes the models homeostatic in terms of neural activity and total synaptic weights.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The RP model is the least structured distribution that retains the average values of the projections and is mathematically unique.
source: Thus, it is the least structured distribution that retains the average values of the projections, is mathematically unique
evidence: This is a mathematical property of maximum entropy distributions.

claim: The RP model proved to be highly accurate in predicting individual activity patterns using small amounts of training data when applied to cortical data from multiple areas.
source: Applied to cortical data from multiple areas (see, e.g. Figure 1A), this model proved to be highly accurate in predicting individual activity patterns, using small amounts of training data (Maoz et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and reference to data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each intermediate neuron in the RP circuit implements one projection of the input population.
source: Each intermediate neuron implements one projection of the input population.
evidence: This is a description of the neural circuit architecture.

claim: Sigmoid RP models outperform step RP models.
source: We first learned the RP model as in Maoz et al., 2020, using a Heaviside non-linearity for the projections, and RP models that used a sigmoid non-linearity, where both models used the same set of RP, and found the latter models to be be more accurate (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative performance data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reshaped RP models outperform RP models for a low number of projections.
source: The reshaped models outperform the RP ones for a low number of projections, whereas the performances of all three models converge to a similar value for large number of projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by the log-likelihood data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The firing rates of neurons in the intermediate layer are considerably lower for reshaped models compared to RP and backpropagation models.
source: Interestingly, the firing rates of the neurons in the intermediate layer are considerably lower for the reshaped models, and this sparseness in activity becomes more pronounced as a function of the number of projections (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The correlations between projections in reshaped models are considerably lower compared to RP and backpropagation models.
source: We further find that the correlations between the projections in the reshaped models are considerably lower compared to RP and backpropagation models (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Optimizing thresholds has a small effect on the performance of Reshaped RP and backpropagation models.
source: We find that this addition has a small effect on the performance of the models in terms of their likelihood (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: For models with large number of projections, low values of λ result in better performance than models with high values.
source: We find an opposite relation for models with large number of projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: For a wide range of synaptic budgets, homeostatic models outperform bounded models.
source: Figure 2B shows the log-likelihood of each model class vs. the total available synaptic budget of the different models: For a wide range of synaptic budgets, the homeostatic models outperform the bounded models, and only for very high values of available synaptic budget, the performance of the bounded models is on par with the homeostatic models.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All bounded constraint models are inferior to the corresponding RP models.
source: Figure 2D shows the performance of the homeostatic and bounded models that are initialized with the same set of RP; all bounded constraint models are inferior to the corresponding RP ones
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All homeostatic constraint models are superior to the corresponding RP models.
source: whereas all the homeostatic constraint models are superior to the RP models (and clearly all the homeostatic models are superior to the corresponding bounded models).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mean firing rates of reshaped projection neurons are lower in homeostatic models compared to bounded models.
source: We further find that the mean firing rates of the reshaped projection neurons, as well as the correlations between them, are lower in the homeostatic models compared to the bounded models (Figure 2E–F), making them more energetically efficient (in terms of spiking activity).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Lower correlations between neurons are consistent with notions of efficient coding by decorrelated neural populations.
source: We recall that this is consistent with the notions of efficient coding by decorrelated neural populations (Barlow, 1961; Olshausen and Field, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on efficient coding.

claim: The overall performance of the model in terms of capturing the population codebook is similar between the 'free' reshape model and different values of synaptic normalization.
source: Figure 3A shows that the overall performance of the model in terms of capturing the population codebook is similar between the 'free' reshape model and different values of synaptic normalization.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Reshaping with normalization or without it drives the projection neurons to converge to similar average firing rate values.
source: Similarly, reshaping with normalization or without it drives the projection neurons to converge to similar average firing rate values (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The distribution of firing rates over different neurons becomes narrower with tighter normalization values.
source: However, the distribution of firing rates over the different neurons becomes narrower with tighter normalization values (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After reshaping, firing rate values converge to similar average values despite different normalization values implying very different initial firing rates.
source: Importantly, while different normalization values imply very different initial firing rates of the projection neurons, after reshaping the values converge to similar average values (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reshaping with normalization implies smaller changes in the reshaping process compared to reshaping without normalization.
source: Moreover, reshaping with normalization implies smaller changes in the reshaping process (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The true and random connectivity models performed very similarly.
source: Surprisingly, the true and random connectivity models performed very similarly (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The full connectivity models are inferior to the true and random connectivity models, except for the case of high model costs.
source: Although the full connectivity model contains the 'ground truth' connectivity, and could recreate the true connectivity by canceling out unnecessary synapses during reshaping – we find that the full connectivity models are inferior to the other models, except for the case of high model costs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mean correlations between projections and mean firing rates of models using true and random connectivity were very similar.
source: The mean correlations between projections at the end of reshaping and the mean firing rates of the models that use the true and random connectivity were also very similar (Figure 4D–E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4D-E.

claim: Different synaptic budgets have a different optimal in-degree for homeostatic reshaped RP models.
source: We found that different synaptic budgets have a different optimal in-degree (Figure 4F), and that the value of the optimal in-degree seems to grow with the total synaptic budget.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Curves for different total synaptic costs seem to coincide and have a similar peak value when measuring efficiency by synaptic cost per connection.
source: We find that curves for different total synaptic costs seem to coincide and have a similar peak value – suggesting an optimal ratio between the total available resources and the number of synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The performance of models using different homeostatic mechanisms is surprisingly similar in terms of the model's likelihood over test data.
source: Figure 5B shows that the performance of the models that use these other homeostatic mechanisms is surprisingly similar in terms of the model's likelihood over the test data
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The different forms of homeostatic regulation result in different reshaped projections.
source: Figure 5E shows the mean rotation angle over 100 homeostatic models as a function of synaptic cost – reflecting that the different forms of homeostatic regulation results in different reshaped projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: All three homeostatic variants show a similar minimal mean rotation angle at the same value of synaptic cost.
source: Interestingly, although the three homeostatic variants show unique rotation angle histograms, they all show a similar minimal mean rotation angle at the same value of synaptic cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity optimizes the efficiency of network models in scenarios of limited resources and random connectivity.
source: Our results suggest a computational role for the experimentally observed scaling or normalization of synapses during learning: In addition to 'regularizing' the firing rates in neural circuits, in our Reshaped RP models, homeostatic plasticity optimizes the efficiency of network models in scenarios of limited resources and random connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing improved efficiency with homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: The similarity of performance of models using different homeostatic synaptic mechanisms suggests a possible universal role for homeostatic mechanisms in computation.
source: Moreover, the similarity of the performance of models that use different homeostatic synaptic mechanisms suggests a possible universal role for homeostatic mechanisms in computation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed similarity in performance across different homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: A universal value of total incoming synaptic weights for neurons results in widely distributed firing rates that converge to a similar average value.
source: The synaptic normalization constraints we used here offer a simple solution: a universal value of the total incoming synaptic weights for the neurons in the circuit (or outgoing ones), results in a widely distributed firing rates of neurons (which may change considerably during the learning), but converge to a similar average value.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed behavior of the models with synaptic normalization.

claim: The shallowness of the circuit implementation of the Reshaped RP model implies that learning does not require backpropagation of information over many layers.
source: The shallowness of the circuit implementation of the Reshaped RP model implies that the learning of these models does not require the backpropagation of information over many layers, which distinguishes deep artificial networks from biological ones.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological plausibility based on the model architecture.

claim: The locality of the reshaping process points to the feasibility of this model in terms of real biological circuits.
source: Moreover, the locality of the reshaping process itself points to the feasibility of this model in terms of real biological circuits.
evidence: This is an inference about biological plausibility based on the local nature of the learning rule.

claim: The biological plausibility is supported by the robustness of the model to the specific connectivity used and to the specific choice of homeostatic mechanism.
source: The biological plausibility is further supported by the robustness of the model to the specific connectivity used for the reshaped models, and to the specific choice of the homeostatic mechanism we used.
evidence: This is an inference about biological plausibility based on the observed robustness of the models.

claim: The homeostatic mechanism used in the models is a form of 'hard' L1 regularization on the sum of the weights.
source: The homeostatic mechanism we focused on here is a form of 'hard' L1 regularization, but on the sum of the weights.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the homeostatic mechanism in terms of regularization techniques.

claim: Homeostatic normalization may be beneficial for artificial neural network architectures.
source: We, therefore, hypothesize that homeostatic normalization may be beneficial for artificial architectures (see, e.g. Zhong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observed benefits in the biological models, with a citation to related work.

claim: Extra-cellular recordings were performed using Utah arrays from populations of neurons in the prefrontal cortex of macaque monkeys performing a direction discrimination task with random dots.
source: Extra-cellular recordings were performed using Utah arrays from populations of neurons in the prefrontal cortex of macaque monkeys performing a direction discrimination task with random dots. For more details see Kiani et al., 2014.
evidence: This describes the experimental data source, supported by citation.

claim: Neural activity was discretized using 20ms bins.
source: Neural activity was discretized using 20ms bins, such that in each time bin a neuron was active ('1') if it emitted a spike in that bin and silent ('0') if not.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing method used.

claim: Recorded data was split randomly into training sets of 160,000 samples and held-out test sets of 40,000 samples.
source: Recorded data was split randomly into training sets and held-out test sets: 100 different random splits were generated for each model setup, consisting of 160,000 samples in the training set and 40,000 in the test set.
evidence: This describes the data splitting procedure used for model training and testing.

claim: The average in-degree of sparse models used was 5, unless specified otherwise.
source: The average in-degree of sparse models used here was 5, unless specified otherwise in the text.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice for the models.

claim: Synthetic neural activity patterns were obtained by training RP models on real neural recordings and then generating data using Metropolis–Hastings sampling.
source: Synthetic neural activity patterns were obtained by training RP models on real neural recordings as described above and then generating data from these models using Metropolis–Hastings sampling.
evidence: This describes the method for generating synthetic data.
